utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that there was a preliminary matter you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Mladic has to be at the UN Detention Unit after our third session, so he will waive his right to be present here, agrees that we continue with the trial, only he -- that the transportation should be organised for him to be transported to the UNDU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have reported this to the Registry --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that they can contact the transport services?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, in view of the fact that there's an explicit waiver, we'll then continue after that. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to deal with the following matter, and that is the testimony of Witness Haglund. On the 24th of June, the Prosecution gave notice of its intention to tender an additional report for expert witness Haglund. The Defence objected to this on the 8th of July and requested that the witness's testimony be delayed, as the current scheduling would not give the Defence the 30 days to review the report as stipulated in the Rules. The Chamber notes that Haglund is scheduled to testify on the 25th of July, thus 31 days after the Prosecution's filing. Furthermore, the Chamber has already ruled on the witness's expertise and indicated that the witness should be brought for cross-examination. Under these circumstances, the Chamber sees no reason to delay the witness's testimony at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Lukic will now cross-examine you. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You'll find him to your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will pose my questions in B/C/S so you receive proper translation and I will wait after that for a while for your answers to be translated. It doesn't mean that I'm not satisfied because I'm pausing.

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we heard from you that you know Mr. Dean Manning. Would you agree with me that Mr. Manning is a lay person and that he's not an expert in your area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Manning is not an expert in my area of expertise or at least he was not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding the tests that you did in the course of your work, it's true that Mr. Manning did not take part in these tests; right?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Manning did not take part in any of those tests that I performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He did not take part in any conclusions or opinions reached on the basis of your tests; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not take part in any of my conclusions or opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning drafted a number of written reports, quite lengthy ones, and he made some observations and conclusions in reporting on the work that you performed. Am I correct if I were to say that you did not help him in the drafting of any of these reports?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen such reports, therefore I've never helped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my following question. I'm going to ask you if it's correct that Mr. Manning never asked you to look at and verify the information contained in his report, at least not in the part that concerned your area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In his testimony, Mr. Manning gave some of his opinions regarding certain strips of fabric that were found in the garbage dump and that were not close to any graves. On page 14269 of our transcript, Mr. Manning said that these strips were not kept because his predecessor, Mr. Jean Rene Ruez, decided to film them with a video camera. As an expert in this field, would you agree that video recording or photographing of fabric would not be the proper way to keep samples that would make it possible for you to conduct tests on them?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Video recording is -- makes it impossible to run any further tests because then you would have to have the textile material itself. We kept from the textiles small pieces of fibre to examine them microscopically, so if there was to be any more tests to be done, then the NFI would still have the small amounts of fibres taken from the textile materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever consulted by Mr. Jean Rene Ruez if it was all right to destroy certain samples of strips of fabric or pieces of clothing?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never consulted by any persons of the ICTY. Maybe -- shortly after I finished those examinations, I left the department. So maybe other persons were consulted but I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had you been asked about destroying strips of fabric or pieces of fabric of clothing, would you have agreed with that, given your permission?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have given my personal opinion what the implications would be of destroying strips of fabric, and I would leave the decision about destroying them with the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What would you have said when giving your personal opinion on this matter?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have pointed out that when destroying the fabric no other tests could be done or no second opinion would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that you did not examine any strips of fabric other than those you identified and that you dealt with in your written report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and my team only examined the strips of fabric that were mentioned in the report, saying what items we received, so it's about 400 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning identified the anthropologists and archaeologists as being the source of information about the origin or source of the fabrics. Madam, in your work to determine the nature of the textiles and the way you reach your conclusions on these samples, would that also include archaeologists and anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made my results and I took the conclusion or I made the conclusion based on the textile and fibre experience that I have and not on any archaeological or anthropological way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I seek clarification on one of the previous answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you and your team "only examined the strips of fabric that were mentioned in the report, saying what items we received, so it's about 400 or so." I did understand from your testimony in chief that you made a selection of what samples you would more thoroughly examine and compare, but you received far more than those that were -- that underwent a very thorough examination. Do I understand that you still kept small pieces of the -- all of the samples you received even those which you did not examine in such detail as the ones you had selected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right, we only took small pieces of fibre from the ones that we thoroughly examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the other ones, is there anything left from that, you said 400?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know now, as I recall, we did not take any fibre samples of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you received the original material, you took some samples to examine thoroughly. What happened with the remainder? Is there anything left out of the other, well, if we could say some 390 or a little bit less, that you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the about 400, we saw macroscopically matching textiles and from those we took extra fibre samples and from the other we did not take any fibre samples and we gave them back to the ICTY without taking fibre samples, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So from the large majority of the material you received, nothing is left with the NFI at -- to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, nothing is left to my knowledge at the NFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to move to your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P1771 on our monitors, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Maljaars, first of all I wanted to ask you this: This report or any other report that you authorised for the needs of this case, was it subjected to any kind of review by your colleagues or, as it's described in English, was it subject to peer review?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was peer reviewed for the information about the textile material and it was peer reviewed for my use of the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was subject to peer review, in terms of the content, the material, and the text, could you please tell us who carried out this review and what did it involve?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The peer review about the content was done by a co-worker at that time and it involved everything, checking numbers, dates, conclusions, anything that I wrote down concerning the investigations. The peer review in English was carried out by a linguistic expert who had a master's degree in English to see whether the terms and the sentences that I used were good enough to work with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you when you're talking about the peer review by the co-worker, is that the same review as you told us about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's part of the same review that I told yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree then that there was no peer review by anyone outside of your lab?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was no peer review by someone outside of the laboratory of the NFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that one person conducted the review. Could you please tell us when the review was completed?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The review of the investigations was completed just before I submitted the report, so it must have been the beginning of February 2000. And I would like to say it says on my screen "the review of the investigations," that would be the investigations of the textiles that's in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This person who conducted internal review, did they provide any kind of written findings, critique, suggestions?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did or she did. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then is that part of this report or not?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those comments are not -- well, those -- we discussed the comments that she made and I made some alterations in the report before submitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many other reports have you prepared during your career, during your work in this laboratory?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to give an estimate. I don't know, maybe a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you provide your findings ever for outside peer review, outside of your institute?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I saw here in your work - and we see the first page of it on our monitor - that you divided the samples that you worked on into five groups. In the first group you described three pieces of textile material -- I apologise, two pieces of textile material; in the second group, three pieces; in the third group, two pieces; in the fourth group, three pieces; and in the fifth group, six pieces. Is that the total number of pieces of textile material that you processed and analysed in the course of the entire process?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The textiles that you mentioned are the ones that were examined more thoroughly based on macroscopical similarities between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we will agree that only these textiles were tested for this report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, all of the textiles were investigated and were described, and only when a macroscopical similarity came up, those pieces of textiles were examined on a microscopical way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "investigated" and "described," [In English] "And only when a macroscopical similarity came up, those pieces of textiles were examined on a microscopical way." [Interpretation] How did you establish microscopic similarity unless you examined them under a microscope? Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there any possible confusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where macroscopical is mixed up with microscopical. I do understand that without using a microscope, just by the bare eye, I take it that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A macroscopic examination, then, would be one that you did with the bare eye and you did not examine those samples microscopically. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is one addition to be made. A macroscopical examination also includes a magnification of about ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From whom specifically did you get the samples? Was it from Mr. Dean Manning?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first batch of textile materials we received from Mr. Ruez, and I think the second one was received from Mr. Dean Manning, although the -- there may have been more persons with them at that time. But we received them from Mr. Ruez and Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I read from yesterday's transcript: "We received them from Mr. Ruez, Mr. Kruszewski and Mr. Manning," so to put the same question to the witness where even I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I missed that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Maljaars, how did you establish the provenance of each sample where told they had been found by someone else?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provenance of each sample, meaning the origin of the sample, was written on papers with codes -- individual codes of the textile material that were in -- well, the batch that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not check the accuracy of this information yourself, nor were you in a position to do so; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those textiles were entered in the laboratory, they were checked by me to see if all the textiles were there and that they had a proper identification code on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I probably didn't phrase my question well. I wanted to ask you whether you checked, whether you were able to check, if a piece of fabric actually came from a given location; in other words, you did not go to the sites, correct?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not go to the sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on to page 8 of your report. It should also be page 8 in e-court. Near the bottom of the page, that is, the third line from the bottom, we read: "B076.5 - ligature/blindfold." Who decided if something was a blindfold or a ligature? Was it you or the investigators who gave you the material?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by the investigators that gave me the material and the description that they provided us with is in the list that's on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the record let me ask you if this applies to all the entries, wherever it says "ligature" or "blindfold"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go to page 11 of your report now. Here we see a description of the procedure and you say there that a database was formed. Was that database created in your institute?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was and it was created by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who entered data in that database, you again?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the data I entered and others were done by a co-worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which data you entered?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Don't you remember or is it -- is this classified information?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. There were over 400 entries and I don't know -- I don't recall which one I made or what was done by a co-worker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question, is it visible in the database who --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- made the entries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can tell you something more about creating the database, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I was just giving a follow-up question. If Mr. Lukic is interested in it, he'll ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there, or rather, did you use a special software or what was the format of that database?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used Microsoft Excel or Access, I can't remember which one of them I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us how many items from each group were examined microscopically. Who decided what would be examined and what not?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I decided what to be examined and what not to be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the exhibit list next to your name we see the Prosecution exhibit, namely P27979.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like for it to be displayed. I'll have some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most likely is that a wrong number. An exhibit number with the number P27979 would bring us somewhere in 2018, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's P1739 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks for your help. Let's try that one. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this document shown to you during the proofing?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember ever having seen this list? I don't mean to say that you should have seen it, but were you involved in the creation of this document in any way?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know this will be a surprise for everybody, but this answer shortens my cross-examination drastically and this is all we had for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Maljaars. This is all we had for you. Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Jeremy, any need to put questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber has also no further questions for you, Madam, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming -- usually I add to that "coming to The Hague," but that might be not the right expression, and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And even though it may not be a very long distance, I nevertheless wish you a safe return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest to the parties that I deal with a few procedural matters, we would then take the break, and then after the break, would the Prosecution be ready to call its next witness? Then a few procedural matters. The first, the Defence submitted on the 9th of July two requests seeking extension of respectively 30, 45, and 30 days to respond to the Prosecution's 28th, 29th, and 30th Rule 92 bis motions on the basis of the length of these respective motions. The Prosecution has indicated that it does not object to reasonable extensions. The Chamber hereby grants the Defence's request. For the 28th and the 30th Rule 92 bis motions, the new response dead-line is the 8th of August, 2013; and for the 29th Rule 92 bis motion, the new response dead-line is the 23rd of August. Then the Defence has submitted a request on the 9th of July of this year, seeking an extension of 14 days to respond to the Prosecution's bar table motion to admit UN Resolutions reports and code cables. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution has indicated that it does not object to reasonable requests for extensions, and the Chamber hereby grants the Defence's request. The new dead-line for the response is set at the 23rd of July. Then I would like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think you omitted the 30th 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. I think I said the 28th and the 30th --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Rule 92 bis motions with the same dead-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would like to deal with the following matter. On the 19th of October, 2012, the Chamber admitted into evidence Witness Mujanovic's statement on the condition that the necessary declaration and attestation pursuant to Rule 92 bis be filed within four weeks of the decision. The Prosecution only filed the requested material on the 16th of January, 2013, long past the dead-line. And the Chamber would like to know whether the Prosecution has any explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't right now. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please inform the Chamber as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next item I would like to deal with is the position of the Defence regarding the verification of transcription for P1451. In court on the 14th of May, the Chamber inquired about the possible transcription error in Exhibit P1451, an excerpt from the testimony of Witness Zlatan Celanovic from the Popovic case. The sentence in question occurs in the original text of the Popovic transcript at page 6635 and in e-court on page 11, lines 24 to 25 of P1451 and reads: "I did thought mention the 28th Division and I didn't know there was a 28th Division." In court on the 16th of May, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that after having checked the corresponding B/C/S audiotape of the transcript, the sentence should correctly read: "I did not mention the 28th Division and I didn't know there was a 28th Division." The Defence informed the Chamber that it would have to verify this and was requested to come back to the Chamber within seven days. In court on the 13th of June of this year, the Chamber inquired again about the Defence's position, but the Defence did not come back to the Chamber. Could the Defence submit its position regarding the transcription for P1451?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously very late, but if we can get one more day. I don't know if somebody checked it, but I don't have the data with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- it's almost time for the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Saved by the bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, saved by the bell, Mr. Lukic. The Chamber happily grants your extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is better than at the point to lose a boxing match, isn't it? But before we take that break I'd like to deal with Exhibits P1674. On the 2nd of July, 2013, transcript page 13700, the Chamber admitted Exhibit P1674 into evidence. This is an unofficial and uncorrected transcript of Drazen Erdemovic's testimony in Prosecutor versus Popovic et al. dated the 4th of May, 2007. The Chamber instructs the Prosecution to upload an official, corrected version of P1674 into e-court and to inform the Chamber when it has done so. The Chamber requests the Registry to then replace the current version with the newly uploaded one. I leave it to that for the time being. We take the break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Prosecution is ready to call its next witness, let me see, we need -- no protective measures requested. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I take it that you want to call Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and we would be requesting a caution for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, as the parties may have noticed, the list of exhibit numbers attached to the admitted evidence of Witness Rupert Smith has been filed by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Obradovic. Before you give your testimony, I would like to invite you to make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Obradovic, I'd like to inform you that you as a witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate yourself. We, then, as a Chamber, we may compel you to nevertheless answer the question, but testimony compelled in that way should not be used as evidence in any subsequent proceedings against you, if there are any, for whatever offence, apart from if you would be prosecuted for giving false testimony. I think it's not the first time that you were informed about this rule. Have you understood the important content of this rule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find him to your right. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you please state your name and current rank?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Ljubomir Obradovic, born in 1950, in Visegrad. I'm retired and I retired with the rank of major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall recently testifying in the Tolimir case here at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was your testimony truthful and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked then, would your answers be substantially the same?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all extra microphones be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answers would be the same in essence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would then like to offer the testimony from the Tolimir trial, 65 ter 29083.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29083 receives number P1783, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if I could, I would deal with the associated exhibits after the testimony, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could, I would like to read a short summary of the witness's testimony; that is purely for the public. In 1992 and 1993, the witness was Chief of Staff and acting commander of a VRS brigade in the 1st Krajina Corps. On 1 September 1994, the witness was transferred to the Main Staff to the position of chief of the operations department within the operations and training administration of the Main Staff. In June 1995 he was promoted to colonel. On 27 January 1995, the witness broke his leg and he returned to duty at the Main Staff on the 17th of July, 1995. He was promoted to general after the war. At the Main Staff he was the deputy of, and directly subordinate to, General Miletic, who was the chief of the operations and training administration. The witness will testify about the structure and functioning of the VRS Main Staff. He will identify the Main Staff's different sectors, administrations and units, including the 67th Communications Regiment, the 10th Sabotage Detachment, the 65th Protection Regiment, and the department of civil affairs and others. He will set out their various duties and responsibilities. He will explain the co-ordination of these sectors, administrations, and units in carrying out their duties. He will testify about the command relationship of the Main Staff and its different components and subordinate units. The witness will testify about the tasks and competencies of the operations and training administration and its role in the preparation, execution, and monitoring of military operations conducted by VRS units. With reference to VRS military documents and military operations, the witness will explain the reporting channels between the Main Staff and its subordinate units and between the Main Staff and the supreme commander. He will comment on the reporting procedures as well as aspects of the information contained in daily combat reports. He will explain what directives are, their significance, and the process involved in their drafting. He will also give evidence about the knowledge and involvement of the VRS Main Staff officers, including Mladic, Miletic, and Tolimir and others in dealings with UNPROFOR and approval and passage of humanitarian and UNPROFOR convoys through VRS-held territory. The witness will additionally comment on a range of orders and reports emanating both from the Main Staff and from subordinate units on various topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, as you know, you've testified in a fair amount of detail in the Tolimir case and a good part of that testimony is now in evidence in this case. So I won't be going over that again in detail, though I do want to bring up a couple of things. And is it true that you first testified at this Tribunal as a Defence witness called in the Miletic Defence in the Popovic et al. case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the Prosecution called you as a witness in the Tolimir case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then not so long ago, the Prosecution called you as a witness in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in February of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And welcome back for hopefully your last time. And I first want to provide something to the Court, it is exhibit 65 ter 25940. It is a line-and-block chart that is referred to in the testimony and so I will not be going over it in detail, but I do want to confirm with you that this is something that you have recently had a chance to review and that you stand by its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it may be easier to hand out the A3 size. I did give one in Serbian to Mr. Lukic, but it's a good thing to have, I think, for this witness, Mr. President. And Ms. Stewart has some copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they could be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could blow that up a little bit and on the staff sector which is over to the left side which, as we can see, does include the administration for operations and training. Could we get the General a copy as well. Yes, they've seen it, they've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a copy for Mr. Mladic as well or has he received one? I have my B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do have an extra one for him. Mr. Lukic has got his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that there's one available for the accused as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, as you -- do you recall me showing this to you yesterday at our offices?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- and I think you had recalled earlier the name of the 67th Communications Regiment person which is blank in this diagram. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was asked by Ms. Edgerton in the Karadzic case about the organisations, I remembered the name of the commanding officer of the communications regiment, that was Colonel Gredo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. And otherwise, does this document look accurate as to your recollection of helping create or fill out the boxes for the Tolimir case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And these -- we see these solid lines coming out of General Mladic's box at the top. One swings around the whole unit and goes down to the corps commanders and to the 10th Sabotage Unit and the air force and anti-defence and military schools. What's the significance of a solid line connecting General Mladic to these people and units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The line implies subordination and superiority by the commander of the Main Staff in relation to sectors of the Main Staffs and the administrations and the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this a direct connection between the commander and the various people and units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Meaning there's nobody or institution in between?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, except if a unit had a reduced number of connections which would be burning the command process, the commander would give those duties to one of the professional organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25940 receives number P1784, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1784 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as I've said, you've talked about these people and units in detail, so I won't get into that. But just one thing, we see your administration over here for operations and training. We see it as headed by General Miletic, of course, with you as the chief of operations. Can you tell us, by design and by - how do you say it? - how many people really were supposed to be in an operations administration as opposed to how many you actually had back in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: By establishment on the basis of which this organisation was established, the operations and training administration was supposed to have 18 staff. And, in fact, the number of staff in the administration was four: General Miletic, as the chief of the administration; myself, as the chief of operations, and I was also General Miletic's deputy at the same time; the chief of the training department, that was the late Colonel Krsto Djeric; and there was also another lieutenant, Micanovic, in my section who was a cartographer. So the staffing level was actually approximately 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the head of the section for training, it's not clear if we have the right name on the transcript. Krsto and what is his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Krsto Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this understaffed problem that you had in your administration a problem that was consistent within the entire Main Staff? Or was it just your -- just operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This was a problem in all the sectors and administrations of the Main Staff, and it featured also in the units because there was a shortage of professional cadres. The staff sector that the administration was a part of had the -- a staffing level of 36 per cent. It was supposed to number 46 people, but actually the level of staffing was 36 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't have any other questions on this, if -- and we'll go on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you also spoke at length about reporting, reporting procedures and such, and I would like just to go to a couple of examples of some of the reports that came into and went out of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could start with exhibit 65 ter 04035.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we just look at that first page in both languages, we can see that this is a report from the Main Staff to the president of the Republika Srpska and the various corps and other units - I won't read them out. And I don't think we need to go to the end, but we'll -- I think all will agree that it's under the name of Major-General Radoje Miletic, standing in for the Chief of Staff, which is something you explained at length in your testimony what that meant. So I would like to go -- as we see and as you've explained, this is a report that goes to the president that talks about the situation in each of the corps. And let's go to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be on page 3 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so we now see it entitled: "In the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps ..." It talks about the enemy. Can you remind us, just briefly, where is the Main Staff getting this information from that it's sending on to the president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: At the reporting organisation, subordinate units of the corps supply their reports or submit their reports to the corps command by a certain time of day. The corps command then collate all of those reports into one report and then they send such a report from the corps to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Based on the reports received from the corps commands, the anti-aircraft defence section and the training schools, the Main Staff would compile a main report which would then be addressed to the president and those persons who were members of the supreme commands, those would be the vice-president, the president of the Assembly, the prime minister, the defence minister, and the minister of the interior. In order to inform subordinate units about events in the whole theatre, we would send the reports also to the corps commands, so in order to inform the subordinate units about the overall situation in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And remind us who assembles all these reports and then creates this report that gets sent to the president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: By establishment, that was the job of the administration for operations and training which had an operations centre within it. That operations centre was in charge of these assignments and it had a chief, two shift leaders, and one operator who entered all the data. We didn't have anyone and this operations centre did not function, and that is why we in the operations department and the training department and frequently we also used superior officers from the branches organ for those jobs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the -- I'm sorry, were you not finished?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: And we would compile the reports from the corps and from the other subordinate units and send it to the address that I -- to the addresses that I referred to, such as the address of the president and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go to the next page in English, it's section (b) in the B/C/S so that can stay where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to look at some of the examples of the kind of information you would get and pass on. So we see here that it mentions the Krivaja 95 task at the top of the page, it says: "All the combat tasks are going ahead as planned. During the day, they liberated Potocari, and they continued advancing in order to liberate all the settlements in the Srebrenica enclave. On the ... axes, part of our units and MUP units have organised ambushes in order to destroy Muslim extremists who have not surrendered and who are trying to break out from the enclave towards Tuzla." Can you help us on this sentence beginning "on the ... axes." That's an unknown word for the translators. So after it says "on the ... axes," can you tell us what is being said there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have the same report in front of me. With -- in my copy it says: "In the Drina Corps from the Srebrenica enclave transport of the population was organised towards Kladanj in the course of the day" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "During the day about 10.000 Muslims are estimated for transport. In all the areas of responsibility of the corps, the situation on the territory is stable and under control. During the day in most populated areas, recruits were being sent off to the army. All the planned and approved convoys passed safely through RS territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I was -- that's okay, General. I was going to ask you about that, but you've just got that out. So -- but it's -- the one I was asking about to help us with the word is the paragraph up above. It's -- should be under (b) for you. It starts "Krivaja 95" and there was just a word in about the third sentence that we couldn't make out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not clear if we have the right part in B/C/S. Under (b) the heading is different or it's the second part of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the second part of (b).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, in the third line it starts with "Krivaja 95."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you could just read slowly where after "Krivaja 95 task ..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please speak in the microphone or could the microphone be adjusted in such a way that the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "During the day they liberated Potocari and they continue advancing in order to liberate all of the settlements in the Srebrenica enclave. On the estimated axes," "procenjenim," "part of our units and MUP units have organised ambushes in order to destroy Muslim extremists who have not surrendered and who are trying to break out from the enclave towards Tuzla" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. There seems to be a practical problem. The portion just read seems to be on the B/C/S version which is now shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, General, is this the kind of information that was normally sent off to the president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The information was about the enemy, the situation in the field, and the proposals from the corps for subsequent operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04035 receives number P1785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Could I ask one question in relation to this document. On page 3 in the B/C/S and 3 in the English, under 5, reference is made in B/C/S which seems to be a corps referred to as HK, in the English as BK. Could you tell us what corps that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is an abbreviation for the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is not immediately clear from the English translation. Yes, it's clear now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, I'd like to go to a Drina Corps report to the Main Staff, one of the daily reports on the next day, the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 04123.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I just want to call your attention to some information on here and then go to the Main Staff to the president report and ask you just a couple of questions. But the information to please focus on is we see here in the third paragraph under "the enemy" that: "The enemy from the former Srebrenica enclave are in total disarray and have been surrendering to the VRS in great numbers." Then if we go down to the section "situation in the zone of responsibility," we see: "The Corps zone of responsibility is under full control. So far the transport of 15.000 Muslims from Potocari to Kladanj has been organised. "In Konjevic Polje and also in Nova Kasaba reception of Muslim civilians and soldiers who surrender is being carried out taken in an organised fashion ..." Okay. And is this one of the reports that you were talking about from the corps to the Main Staff that gets assembled by your unit and then finds its way into the report to the president in some form?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04123 receives number P1786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1786 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we could go to 65 ter 04038, which should be that Main Staff report to the president on the 13th of July. And if we can again go to the Drina Corps section, which should be page 3 in the English. It's noted as paragraph 6. And page -- same page 3. And we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could just read that to yourself to see if we can find the information that was in the Drina Corps report, and I'll help us a bit as you're reading that because you may remember from the Drina Corps report there was a paragraph that said "the enemy from the former Srebrenica enclave are in total disarray and had been surrendering to the VRS in great numbers ..." And if we look at that first paragraph, we eventually see a sentence in the current document, and I quote: "The enemy from the former enclave of Srebrenica is in a state of total disarray, and the troops are surrendering in large numbers to the VRS ..." And as we continue to look down, we -- I'll remind us that from the Drina Corps report it noted that the: "Corps zone of responsibility is under full control. So far the transport of 15.000 Muslims from Potocari to Kladanj has been organised ..." And then in the Drina Corps report it goes on to say: "In Konjevic Polje and also in Nova Kasaba, reception of the Muslim civilians and soldiers who surrendered is being carried out taken in an organised fashion." In this Main Staff report to the president, I don't see anywhere any reference to the surrender of Muslim civilians. That information is not being passed on to the president that was received from the Drina Corps. Can you -- I know you weren't there at the time, but can you think of any reason why this information was left out of the report that came to them in the Drina Corps report?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I can only speculate. Could this be scrolled down? Perhaps I can see the initials of the one who wrote this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The initials of the person who compiled the report are NT. I believe that stands for Nikola Trkonja [as interpreted]. In the report of the Drina Corps, after the mention of 200 or 300 fighters there was an addition about Muslims. I don't know why it was left out. In the paragraph about the situation in the territory, in this report we see a mention of Kladanj and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We heard that you said I think Niko Trkulja. Is it Niko or Nedjo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, it's Nedeljko Trkulja. I correct myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04038 receives number P1787, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1787 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as a career JNA and VRS officer, were you familiar and are you now familiar with what a directive is in the context of the VRS and the RS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: A directive is a combat document about which I was taught and I knew from the theory that prevailed in the former army. It's also the same in the VRS. It's a combat document that emanates from high-ranking commands. It regulates all essential matters in connection with the planning and implementation of combat operations during a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say upper echelons make these, who would that be in the context of the VRS and RS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In the VRS the Supreme Command is a high command and also the command of the Main Staff. When I say "combat documents of high commands and staffs," this is the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in some of the directives that are in this case, we have seen General Mladic's signature, others such as Directive 7 the Court has seen President Karadzic's signature. Do you know why that is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Directive number 7 signed by President Karadzic was drafted after an analysis was conducted of combat-readiness for the year 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I appreciate that and I -- this is a question I don't know if you can answer, but do you know why some directives are signed by Karadzic and others by Mladic? And we'll get a bit into Directive 7 after that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This was only meant to be an introduction into the answer to your question. The civilian leadership was involved in this analysis of combat-readiness and the head of the civilian leadership was the supreme commander. The first directive that ensued after that analysis was signed by the supreme commander. Directive 7/1, although I wasn't involved in drafting either, was signed by the commander of the Main Staff because it was a directive concerning subsequent operations. I believe that it was written in late March, on the 31st or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what is the particular purpose for these directives? And remind us, first of all, where the directive goes and then what their purpose is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago when I defined what a directive is, perhaps I should explain. Directives include tasks and deal with matters that concern corps. It's written for a longer period of time. It doesn't go much into detail. Objectives are stated there. So that corps commands have a kind of orientation about the tasks that are expected to follow through a certain period and they can prepare in every way for what is stated in the directive. Operations that are to be implemented at the level of the army, including the involvement of the Main Staff, are mentioned there, just as operations supposed to be implemented independently by corps commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break now. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, are you on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear. We take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity for the following. The Defence has submitted a request on the -- yesterday, on the 15th of July, for a 30-day extension to file its response to the Prosecution's 31st 92 bis motion on the basis of the length of the motion. The Prosecution has indicated recently that it does not object to reasonable extensions, and for that reason the Chamber hereby grants the Defence request and sets a new dead-line of the 14th of August for filing a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, in the past you've described that there's two methods in putting together a directive, a full and an abbreviated. Could you briefly explain to us the two methods.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The full method involves all staff organs, that is, sectors and administrations. The abbreviated method does not involve all, hence the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to Directive 7, which is Exhibit P01469. And I know you have talked about this before in I think all your testimonies. And can you tell us, did you ever see this directive while you were at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I told you in the Miletic case that looking for some documents in a cabinet when ordered to do so, I came across a document and took a cursory look at it. It may have been in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think you said you were -- you found it in General Miletic's strong-box or lock-box?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It was a metal cabinet and I took a cursory look because I had no time to deal with it. My task was to fetch another document for Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So whose lock-box or cabinet was this that you found the document in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure now. It may have been the Chief of Staff's cabinet or the cabinet of the entire staff sector, because it contained documents of the training administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's -- let's go to the next page in the document. This is the letter that you will recall, Your Honours, that went with the document that has always been attached on the front of it. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this the Directive 7 that you've talked about before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we go to the last page in both documents, the signature page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that this was -- at the bottom it says: "Drafted by: Colonel Radivoje Miletic. "Typed by: Staff Sergeant Spasoja Zeljkovic." We know who Miletic is. This Staff Sergeant Zeljkovic, what unit was he assigned to at this time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Staff Sergeant Spasoja Zeljkovic was in the establishment structure of the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the logistics -- in the logistics sector, that was Djukic's sector?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, based on your knowledge of Directive 7, was it put together in the full method by all the organs or the abbreviated method?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Based on its structure and layout, I think that the full method was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you describe for us in brief, as you did in Tolimir, the process of doing this? You may recall in Tolimir you said that General Mladic started the proceedings and then heard from various people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This specific directive, having been written soon after the analysis of combat-readiness for the previous year, all those involved in that analysis, especially corps commanders, made proposals in the conclusion about the tasks for the subsequent period. The leadership and the Supreme Command, as well as the Main Staff, must have spoken about it, must have discussed it, and defined the relevant tasks in accordance with the situation in the theatre of war. Based on that, the individual sectors continued to further elaborate their respective fields or parts of the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "leadership" - let me interrupt for a second - do you include General Mladic in that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: To my surprise, the commander of the Main Staff was not a member of the Supreme Command, but it's a fact nonetheless. The Supreme Command comprised the president of the republic, the vice-presidents, the prime minister, the president of the Assembly, the minister of defence, and the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, General, we understand that. What was General Mladic's involvement in the Directive 7, the process of creating the directive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about Directive 7 because I wasn't present and I don't know the methodology. If we're to speak about Directive 7/1 signed by him, then it would have been -- would have had to be him who approved the parts put together by the sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we can see that this document was drafted by Mladic's chief of operations and training and the Court has seen this document and has seen the various contributions that have gone into it. Based on your knowledge of how the Main Staff worked, what would General Mladic's role have been in the creation of this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I can only repeat that I don't know about this directive number 7, but I can suppose what his role was with regard to Directive 7/1 signed by him. I don't know who was involved in drafting this directive here. In the heading we saw "Supreme Command" or "supreme commander" and it was signed by the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the Main Staff involved in this document in any way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I assume so because the Supreme Command and the civilian leadership did not have the professional staff to cover all of the segments of the directive. So the participation of the organs or the sectors and administrations of the Main Staff was inevitable. As for specific people from which sector, which administration, that's something that I don't know except for what I read at the bottom, Zeljkovic and Miletic and the president who signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to something you said in the -- I believe it was the Popovic case, 65 ter 29092, e-court page 39. And I'll read the question. I say: "Thank you. General, I am just trying to get a -- what should be the normal path of this directive," and that would be Directive 7, "before it gets finally signed off by Karadzic. So if Milovanovic is there, you say he's a stickler for detail, he wants to see it. Would Mladic want to see it as well if he was there before it goes to the president, or would he see it under the rules that you were living by?" And your answer was: "According to procedure, General Miletic should have shown the proposal of the directive to the commander, if the Chief of Staff was not there, before sending it off to Karadzic." Then I ask: "Okay. And if the Chief of Staff was there, and he showed it to the Chief of Staff, will it still be seen by Mladic, in your view, under the way the procedures -- and you know General Mladic better than we do." Your answer was: "According to procedure, the Chief of Staff would be duty-bound to show it to General Mladic of course, yes." Do you stand by that -- those answers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, when we're talking about the methodology of the work I stand by that and the responsibilities of the superiors towards the work of their subordinates. As for what really happened is something that I can only speculate about, though, because I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to another subject, brief subject. You may remember Miletic's lawyer Nenad Petrusic asking you that when you were at the Main Staff on the 17th of July, whether Miletic said anything to you about a job for Trkulja, do you remember that and your response to Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was about Trkulja or about a group. He told me that pursuant to the commander's order he sent some senior officers to the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility I think because of some situation that was unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to be clear, who told you this, the commander had sent senior officers to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Miletic told me that pursuant to a task set by the commander he sent Trkulja. I asked about somebody and he said he went on an assignment to the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was this on the 17th, your first day back?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 29091, e-court 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this still the same subject, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I've got off Directive 7, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you asked the witness whether he remembered something he said in another case. And then to -- what's -- the question was what the response was. And then the question is about whether it was him or a group and that "pursuant to the commander's order he sent some senior officers to the Zvornik Brigade ... of responsibility." To say that it's quite clear to me at this moment, no, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's not -- it is not clear, that's why I'm going to the record to try to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the record is about the same matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes -- this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, this -- we are on the same subject to try to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we would start at line 7 and Mr. Petrusic says -- sorry, let's start at line 4. "Q. And what about General Milovanovic, was he there at the General Staff at the time?" And your answer is: "On the 17th, no, he was not." The next question is: "Could you please answer the previous question and tell us what General Miletic told you about Colonel Trkulja upon your arrival in the Main Staff?" And you were talking about on the 17th. And you say: "He told me that he had sent him together with some other officers of the Main Staff upon the order of the commander of the Main Staff to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade." So does this refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that he told me because I was actually inquiring about Trkulja, and he told me that pursuant to an order by the commander he sent him to the Zvornik Brigade because of some unclear situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you inquired about Trkulja, the -- that first day you got back; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon, when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. All right. One last short topic, I hope. I -- you have spoken at length about the convoy requests as you received them from UNPROFOR and others, General Mladic's role in that, and you were -- and you've identified his initials on certain documents. I want to show you one more of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's exhibit 65 ter 19040. And here we see the cover page of a document from the Main Staff dated 31 March 1995, and it lists 14 separate convoy requests from UNPROFOR requesting the Main Staff to approve them. And let's now go to -- it should be in the original B/C/S, e-court 13, and 16 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And like I've done many times before, can I direct your attention ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think Ms. Stewart just spotted it. In the English it goes from 7 to 9, that should be obviously an 8. But this handwriting that we see in the document, the original document on the left, could that be blown up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise that initial?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are General Mladic's initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's the circled word next to his initials?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It says "no," meaning not approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've explained this system and what this means in the transcript, so I don't think - unless the Court has any questions - I will go through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I would offer that whole packet of materials into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19040 receives number P1788, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1788 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Is the Defence ready to start its cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just need one minute to organise myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Obradovic, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Obradovic, good day.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have already heard this before. We spoke the same language, so can I please ask you to pause between question and answer for the interpretation. We need to cover a lot. I will try to make my questions as concise as possible and I kindly ask you to make your answers the same. I'm going to make a small introduction and ask you: How did it come about that in the JNA, before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was mostly the Serbs that were in the army? In other words, did anybody force the non-Serbs in the JNA to leave the army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody forced anyone to do anything. The political leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia and then of the HDZ and the SDA in Bosnia and Herzegovina in support of the idea of secession of the two northern republics, Slovenia and Croatia, and pursuant to the concept of Franjo Tudjman to create a Serbo-Communist or a Serbo-Chetnik army influenced the population of their own ethnic groups not to respond to the summonses to mobilisation and encourage the recruits not to go to the units where they were supposed to report to, and that is why the ethnic structure of the Yugoslav People's Army was disrupted, which always had a certain number of percentages set according to the percentages of specific ethnic groups within the federal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, now I would like to move to the war years and I would like to ask you that when you were in the Krajina, what was the situation therein? In which sector of the Krajina front were you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: If you're thinking of 1994, I went pursuant to a request by the Chief of Staff who left to go there about a month before that, or rather, when the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the Bihac enclave and the Cazin Krajina made two deep incursions towards Krupa na Uni and to the south towards Skender Vakuf. And that was the reason for the commander of the Main Staff to order that a forward command post should be organised, headed by his deputy, in order to stabilise the situation in that sector of the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time was Bihac a safe zone or a protected zone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of many.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the Bosnia and Herzegovina army launch any actions from that area, from the protected zones?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can we conclude then that Bihac was not demilitarised? Our legal questions might sometimes seem superfluous, but this is for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, it was not because the units from that sector, from Bihac, made incursions and created attacks and incidents directed at positions of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time was there any fighting in the Bihac part of Bosnia and Herzegovina between the opposing Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: At that time this inter-Muslim conflict was going on between the forces of the 5th Corps of the B&H Army and forces headed by well-known politician Fikret Abdic, who organised the autonomous province centred on his birthplace of Kladusa where there was also an industrial facility that he managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now going to move to a different topic. I'm going to ask you something about the situation when the commander of the Main Staff is absent. In the event that the commander of the Main Staff is not at the Main Staff, who would replace him? Who would stand in for him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In the absence of the commander at the Main Staff, his deputy by establishment would stand in for him if he is present, that is, the chief of the sector for staff affairs, Lieutenant-General Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if General Milovanovic is not there either, who would take up these duties then? Who decides who would replace him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
