utterances.text: If the chief of the staff sector was absent as well, then before he would leave, the commander of the Main Staff would allocate one of his assistants to do that job. That could be the chief of the morale, legal, and religious affairs, chief of logistics, chief of the organisational, mobilisation, and personnel affairs, or chief of the intelligence and security sector; or if none of them were present, then it would be the chief of the administration for anti-aircraft defence or of the other independent administration, that would be the chief of the administration for plans, development, and finances. So these are the chiefs of sectors who at the same time are assistants to the commander, and then the commander would allocate one of them to replace him. And if all of them were not there, then that would be the duty of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly look at 1D1132.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is your testimony from the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we get a list when you can send it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't receive a list? [Interpretation] Page 11 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the commander of the Main Staff leaves the RS, what is the situation like? I'll read it out for us starting from line 15. The Prosecutor asked you a question. I'll read it out your answer in English. [In English] "And how was the term 'absent' defined? We -- for example, we see General Mladic going to Serbia, going to Belgrade. Would that be considered an absence or would he still be the commander in full command and Milovanovic would still be Chief of Staff? "A. He would temporarily stand in for the commander during the commander's absence." [Interpretation] I'll get back to the question itself, but first tell me if it is true that nobody can be commander in a situation when communication is not possible. In other words, is it a requirement that any commander wishing to exercise command must have means of communication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This subject context is crucially important. Could the next two questions and answer also be read to the victim -- the victim, the witness so that we can nail down this term "absent" a bit better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps we read the next questions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I will. "Q. Would going to Serbia be considered absent? "A. It doesn't depend on the whereabouts of the commander but it depends on the duration of absence."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to do this later, but now I've read it and we have it on the record. So let me ask you if it's a requirement that a person capable of exercising command must have means of communication available?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mobile communications centres are organised for commanders to enable them to exercise command while moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Without these means of communication, the commander cannot exercise command and the same goes for command and control documents; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The abbreviation for that is TKT, classified command documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, since it has been read ... Witness, you said: "It doesn't depend on the whereabouts of the commander but it depends on the duration of absence." What duration would result in temporarily standing in by the deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in previous trials I explained the procedure. If anybody for reasons of physical absence or illness would be uncapable of exercising command, then the superior commander would issue an order about who stands in for that person. The other person appointed in that order - and usually it's the superior officer - assumes all rights and obligations that go with that position. Also that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that person gets all the rights that go with the status in the new position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you during what would be the period of the duration of the absence which would trigger this formal being replaced? Would it be half -- a day, two days, a week, one hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A week or more, to my mind, because if somebody leaves for a day, standing in for the commander is reduced to become present in the command of the staff because the one standing in, because of his position in the establishment or pursuant to a decision by the commander, that person is responsible for order and discipline and the organisation of work inside the staff but has no right to take decisions or issue orders. The deputy in establishment -- in the establishment structure can but only following an approval of the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would then be by remote communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said a deputy in the establishment structure can, but only following an approval of the commander of himself. Would that -- approval obtained from a distance or would it be approved before the commander left, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You misunderstood me. The deputy in the establishment structure can issue an order that is in keeping with the spirit of an earlier decision made by the commander but cannot make new decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore the commander who was absent still is in command although his deputy being present would follow-up on any earlier decisions taken by the commander; is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For a deputy to stand in for the commander, no written order or notice is required; right? General Mladic could simply call General Milovanovic and tell him, "I'm leaving for Belgrade. Now you take over"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if the absence exceeds the duration that I stated, then an order about standing in will be issued and then the deputy will have all the -- the same authority as the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if the absence is shorter than seven days, a written order is not required?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if I understand you well, during such a shorter absence, the deputy who takes over temporarily, short period of time, could not - as you told us - decide but only could follow-up on decisions earlier taken by the commander. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear General Mladic -- did you hear from colleagues upon your return to the Main Staff in July 1995 that the prisoners from Srebrenica were being killed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, not until this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the war, the superior officer is duty-bound to control the work of his subordinates; however, was it easy to replace persons at that time if they were making mistakes as subordinates?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, in both peace and war the superior officer is duty-bound to monitor the work of his subordinate. And when the Prosecutor asked me and I spoke about the share in percentages, I had -- I replied that we had problems with staffing at all levels. And if you were to punish someone by removing him from his position, then you would have to bring in someone new and you don't have anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there problems with reporting in writing during the war? I mean the quality of the reports and I'll show you some documents.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In my previous testimonies, I also spoke about this when asked. There were many inaccuracies in reporting. Sometimes that was a consequence of the poor qualifications of the personnel at lower levels and sometimes it would be the result of the intentions of a commander to hide his responsibility for something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do give us an example.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Here's an example for such intention. In 1994, when I joined the Main Staff, it was in October, Lieutenant Boro Djurdjevic, who hails from the area south of Teslic, came to the Main Staff and met me there. Since I had come from that area on the 1st of September, I asked him what was new back home. And he started listing that everything had been taken, Vucja Glava, Banici, Djukici, and other villages. And I replied that it wasn't right for him to spread misinformation because only the previous evening I was writing a report for the Supreme Command and I never found such information in the report received from the 1st Krajina Corps. He pointed out that he was speaking in all seriousness. I informed General Miletic of that. After a short while he summoned me to the office of the Chief of Staff where he was. And he demanded that I repeat the same in the presence of General Milovanovic. When I did, General Milovanovic called General Tolimir and asked him if he had any information along his own professional lines. The reply was negative. He called the chief of security of the 1st Krajina Corps on the phone. It was Colonel Stevo Bogojevic. He asked him if that information was true. The other replied that it was. When General Tolimir told him to write a report in our presence, he replied, "I can't. But why? Because of the commander." That's an example for the intention to hide something for fear of being reprimanded. Every once in a while we sent out letters to subordinate commands complaining of the poor quality of the reports we were receiving from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 25928 from the Prosecution list, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that this is a document of the Main Staff of the VRS from June 1993, signed by Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic, Chief of Staff. He orders: "1. Send combat reports daily ... as regulated before. "2. Before combat reports are sent, they must be checked and signed by the Commander ..." And then: "3. Keep combat reports brief, clear, meaningful, in accordance with the established standards of military terminology ..." This was in 1993. Did that problem persist later, 1994/1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document. [In English] Your Honour, we would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25928 receives number D331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, we are close to the point where we take a break -- well, we'll take a break and we -- I do understand Mr. Mladic wants to be excused from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness already be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Obradovic. Meanwhile, the Chamber was informed that P1674 has been uploaded now in its official, corrected version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that Madam Registrar can replace the previous copy by this one. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I could help fix a problem you pointed out yesterday about 65 ter number 09670 regarding General Smith's issues. And I can inform you that in the amalgamated report now in evidence at page 785 this document is referred to -- the Prosecution can tell you that this -- this number is ERN 00902180-00902180, and it's -- this ERN number is referenced in the first sentence of paragraph 130 on page 33 of the English version of P785. So I hope that helps resolve your difficulty in finding the reference. That's what I'm provided for by Ms. Stewart, though I didn't say it very eloquently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have to look it up first to see whether it helps, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it looks like an exchange of phone numbers rather than -- but it's appreciated that you paid attention to it. We take a break and we'll resume in the absence of Mr. Mladic at 25 minutes to 2.00. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. We'll continue. Mr. Mladic has waived explicitly his right to be present for this last session this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we look at 1010 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is 1010, Mr. Lukic? Is that an ID number -- a 1D number or is it a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm reading the wrong number from Popovic trial. We need 65 ter 25929.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you yourself told us, this document from 1994 indicates that once again the poor utility of regular combat reports is being pointed to and it also states here that it's a warning, where Major-General Milovanovic, the Chief of Staff, warns -- actually, it's not clear to me. I can see the 2nd Krajina Corps and then again the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the Eastern Bosnia Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, the Drina Corps --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning there is item 1 -- actually, at the beginning it says 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, so the 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is precisely the clarification that I was seeking from you. And based on the content of this document, is it true that the complaint is still about the poor use of regular combat reports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a constant complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25929 receives number D332, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In connection with your stay in the Krajina, if you were to receive an order from General Milovanovic and if he would not be there, did you report back to Miletic instead of to Milovanovic, and did General Milovanovic ask you to visit General Miletic and report directly to him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: My status at the forward command post of the Main Staff was of a temporary nature, lasting for as long as the forward command post was there. So in that position I was directly subordinated to General Milovanovic in terms of the execution of those assignments, but by establishment and status-wise my immediate superior was still General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the transcript I just wanted to record a part of your testimony from the Tolimir case and then I wanted to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 1D1132. Could we look at page 20, please, bottom of the page, line 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will be reading in English again and you will receive translation. Actually, I will begin from line 20 so that we can also see the question. [In English] "Q. If you were given a task by, for example, Milovanovic when Miletic was absent, would you be reporting back to General Miletic, and would he be monitoring your work even though Milovanovic had given you the order? "A. In practice, when the second in command issues a task, I proceed to carry the task out, but I have to report to my immediate superior as to what kind of task I had been given by the second in command or the second superior. There were lots of problems with writing reports. For example, General Milovanovic wanted me to give him reports, bypassing General Miletic. And the other officers were the same. They were not subordinated to Miletic. In other words, General Milovanovic would be the one to inspect such reports and sign them. "Q. But did you go through Miletic as the -- what you've identified as the proper order, proper chain of following those orders? "A. However, if he was not present physically and if priority and speed were required, then I would go directly to the person who had issued the order in the first place." [Interpretation] So other officers as well followed this sequence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think that things are a little bit mixed up here. I was at the forward command post in a kind of resubordinated status to my second-ranking superior, but it was an operational kind of task. So I didn't have any need to keep calling on the telephone and ask to talk to my first immediate superior and tell him I am sending a report from the forward command post or I toured such and such a unit. But generally in practice, according to the rules that we followed, if I receive an assignment directly from the second superior in line, I have to report to him but I have to report to my immediate superior what task I got that did not come from him. But this is something that would not prevent me from carrying out such an assignment. And here specifically reports are mentioned. We wrote reports, Krsto Djeric and I, we were directly subordinated to General Miletic. But these chiefs of combat arms also wrote reports from the combat arms administration but they were not subordinated to Miletic but they were directly subordinated to General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you something about the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to look at 65 ter 25930 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment of the 23rd of December, 1993. The heading is: "Writing of regular combat reports, order." It's signed by the commander of the regiment. At that time that was Major Savcic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the document states: "Based on a verbal order by the chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska," that's General Milovanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "... on writing regular combat reports, in future, regular reports will not be written but the regiment Chief of Staff will call Colonel Miletic on the telephone. And every day at 0800 hours and at 1900 hours on extension 277 the report will be given verbally on issues pertaining to the regular combat report." Was the practice adopted then for the protection regiment not to send in written combat reports anymore?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is probably a consequence of the fact that the regiment command was directly at the location where the Main Staff was. It was engaged for security. It was of different composition so that writing and coding the report would create an even more difficult situation for the encryption personnel. So the Chief of Staff probably wanted to ease their duties a little bit so that the Chief of Staff of the regiment was then supposed to call in and speak to General Miletic every day on extension 277 for that reason. As for the way a report should be written, well, this is an order by Colonel Savcic for his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25930 receives number D333, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, when you earlier, transcript page 59, line 10, referred to 1D1132, where you read part of it, for those following the proceedings at a later stage that what you read is also found in P1783, which is the 92 ter materials of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I composed my questions before I had these excerpts so I was not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- whether I would have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where you didn't oppose admission of it, so therefore it shouldn't have come as a surprise. But it's just to make life easier for those who will read the transcript later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you explained today that you didn't have an operations centre at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You explained who actually did that, and we agreed that finally the reports coming from the corps ended up in General Milovanovic's hands?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for him to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, when General Milovanovic was in Krajina - in other words, he was absent from the Main Staff - we often saw that next to the signature there was the remark "for," that is, somebody else signed for him. Do you know whether General Milovanovic ever corrected those reports because he found some irregularities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: When I had just arrived, I noticed that the combat arms organ or somebody else would submit reports that were returned because of grammatical errors and so on. So I strove to write the reports as accurately and well as possible so that after a while when he saw that my reports were mostly all right, he didn't pay so much attention to these things anymore. Apart from that, in the signature block there was also the remark "standing in for." I explained that earlier and how it came about because General Miletic never stood in for the Chief of Staff when he was in a territory controlled by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I just -- to clarify -- I think your question was based on "standing in," "zastupa," as opposed to "for." Because his answer referred to "standing in" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was "for."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a situation when it was -- when General Milovanovic's name was stated before "standing in for" and in front of General Milovanovic's name there was the word "for," and in case such a letter was sent out by fax or telefax or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- or by telex, you could only see the typed name of General Milovanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The remark "for" and the signature of the person were for authenticating that document. But the communications operator who typed that letter to be sent by telex, for example, would only type the name without the signature itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps it's an interpretation problem. Your last question, page 33, line 25, and the beginning of page 64 -- oh, I said "page 33," that was wrong, page 63. It seems to be that there is a mixture now of "standing in for" and "for." Can you please clarify with the witness. In my view there is a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from that, could you assist me, Mr. Lukic, by giving the page number for where the standing in is explained because I can't find it that quickly in this not-searchable copy. The witness referred to it in his previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was my question so I don't have it in front of me. I was asking "for."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, but since the witness testified about his previous testimony explaining "standing in," I would like to have a possibility to look at it and I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can give it to you tomorrow when we continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, about the signature block, when it says "for," that also applied in case of the signature of General Mladic, often a telefax would feature General Mladic's name. Was anybody in the position to sign a document in his stead --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This continues to confuse the distinction between "for" and "standing in," because that sounds like you're making a reference to the "standing in" and calling it a "for." Each of these documents is different, I think the meanings are different, and this is just confusing it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I am confusing anybody. It wasn't my intention. I'm only dealing with the version "for." I'm not dealing with "standing in."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is at least a clear statement. Now see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that General Mladic was often absent from the Main Staff because he went to various locations on the front line?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the document reads: Colonel-General or Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic and then there's the handwritten remark "for" as well as the signature of the person authorised to act in that manner during a certain period, whereas the other party in the communication only receives a typed copy of the document without the handwritten signature of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This clarifies this matter now. Now tell us whether it's true whether -- that General Mladic often was absent from the Main Staff to visit various locations on the front line?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he often wanted to see for himself what the situation was like in some places. He chose those places himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We only have a few minutes left. Let us speak about directives now. Directive 7 and 7/1, you were asked about them by the Prosecutor today. Is it true that a directive is both military and a political document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's true because the first item of the directive contains a description of the military political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were never involved in the drafting of any directive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean -- what do you mean by "no"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I was never involved in the drafting of any directive, not one of a total of eight or nine that were drafted in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that parts of directive are implemented at a subsequent time and other parts never?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In a directive, tasks and objectives are set very ambitiously. It is normal that as a consequence a substantial part is never implemented. And when a subsequent directive is drafted, then a part of a previous directive can be taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Speaking about which, let me ask you that if a part of Directive 4 has -- is not implemented but not included in Directive 5, is it still valid?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever a new directive is issued, the previous directive is no longer in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1469, please, that's Directive 7. Could we have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the cover letter, followed by the directive as you saw. I would like to deal with page 17 in B/C/S and page 10 in English. The difference is due to many blank pages in the original. We're always interested in the parts where the Drina Corps is mentioned. Here at the beginning it says: "Enemy breakthroughs along selected operative tactical lines should be prevented by extremely persistent and active defence in co-operation with [indiscernible] the forces," et cetera. Do you know that Krivaja 95 was an operation of the Drina Corps and that there was no link-up with the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In keeping with that, is it also true, since it was their operation, that the command of the Drina Corps was able to decide to implement that operation the way it thought best fit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: A directive only states which operation should be implemented, whereas planning is in the remit of the corps command, and that includes the ways of reaching an objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We're at the end of today's hearing. We'll have to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We will conclude for the day, but before I invite you to follow the usher, Mr. Obradovic, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way to whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony that you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 17th of July, in this same courtroom, III, at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of July, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
